# Census That Names Its Own Gaps

When enumerating a large collection — subjects in an archive, tables in a warehouse, endpoints
in an API — the failure that matters is not a wrong entry. It is a **missing** one, and a
missing entry is invisible by definition.

The pattern: pair the enumeration with a hand-maintained disposition map, and make the tool
**print by name every item with no disposition**.

```python
missing = [key for key, _ in rows if key not in COVERAGE]
if missing:
    print(f"\n{len(missing)} entries without a disposition:")
    for key in missing:
        print(f"  {key}")
```

A clean run is now evidence. Not because the author remembered everything, but because anything
forgotten is printed.

## Why a README sentence is not the same thing

"All subjects have been reviewed" is unfalsifiable and drifts silently the moment a new folder
appears. The census re-runs, finds the new folder, finds no entry for it, and says so — which
turns [[documentation-drift]] from something you notice eventually into something the next run
reports.

Same instinct as [[verify-the-load-dont-declare-it]] and [[generated-audit-artifact]]: don't
assert the property, compute it, and let the computation fail loudly.

## What it caught here

The first run reported **17 entries without a disposition**. Seven were empty subject folders
whose names implied material that does not exist; two were film-subtitle archives; one was a
folder whose name is a soft hyphen. None of them was knowingly skipped and none would have been
noticed by rereading the index.

The deeper catch was structural. An earlier census walked *subdirectories* to enumerate
subjects, which is the obvious approach and is wrong for this archive: one semester has no
subject folders at all and 116 files sit loose at its root. Counting loose files at every root
moved the total from 16,066 files to 54,034.

Both numbers were produced honestly. The first excluded what it could not classify and did not
say so, and that is the failure mode this pattern exists to make impossible.

## The two-number rule

A related habit, from the same repository's archive-integrity check: when a check can be read
two ways, report both numbers separately rather than one reassuring one.

```
files newer than the freeze : 94
of which are content        : 0
```

Ninety-four files did change. None of them was content — all were `.git` and `.gradle` metadata
touched by inspection tooling. Collapsing that into "the archive is unmodified" would have been
false; collapsing it into "94 files changed" would have been alarming and useless. The script
fails only on the second number and prints both — [[provenance-and-limits-stated-inline]].

## When to reach for it

Any time a claim of completeness is going to be made about a set that someone else will trust,
and especially when items are added to that set by a process outside your control. The
disposition map is the cost; it is small, and it is the only part that a reviewer needs to read.

## Where this appears

[[pwr-subject-notes]], covering an eight-semester coursework archive. The same shape, applied to
source repositories rather than to subjects, is what `verify-sources` does for this wiki: it
skips directories it cannot verify and *reports* them, because a stray directory passing the
gate silently would make "all source trees clean" mean less than it says.
